curriculum.lesson_evidence: Index notation writes repeated factors: a^n means n factors of a (for positive integer n). Base is a; exponent (index) is n. Expand and evaluate small cases carefully with negatives using brackets: (−2)^4 vs −2^4.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Expand and evaluate 5^3 and (−3)^2; also evaluate −3^2 and explain the difference.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 125; 9; −9 because −3^2 means −(3^2).

WATCH FOR
Ignoring brackets around a negative base. Notation changes the value.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
3^4 = 3×3×3×3 = 81. (−2)^3 = −8. Note: −2^4 = −(2^4) = −16, while (−2)^4 = 16.

TRY FIRST
Expand and evaluate 5^3 and (−3)^2; also evaluate −3^2 and explain the difference.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 125; 9; −9 because −3^2 means −(3^2).
teach_steps.explain:
Index notation writes repeated factors: a^n means n factors of a (for positive integer n). Base is a; exponent (index) is n. Expand and evaluate small cases carefully with negatives using brackets: (−2)^4 vs −2^4.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the places, values or distances that carry the method. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your working with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your reasoning? If a digit or place is uncertain, identify what would have to be regrouped or counted again. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Ignoring brackets around a negative base. Notation changes the value. Correct the value or method, not just the appearance of the digits.
